clinicalPearls: Produces brief, severe, lancinating pain felt deep within the ear (auditory canal and periauricular region)
Attacks may be provoked by touching a trigger zone in the external auditory canal, by swallowing, or by cold stimuli
It can be accompanied by autonomic and sensory phenomena such as altered taste, salivation, lacrimation, and tinnitus, reflecting the wider functions of the nervus intermedius
The nervus intermedius is the sensory and parasympathetic component of the facial nerve, and geniculate neuralgia is essentially neuralgia of this nerve
A viral (herpetic) aetiology is recognised, and it may follow Ramsay Hunt syndrome
Diagnosis requires exclusion of other causes of deep ear pain and overlaps clinically with glossopharyngeal and trigeminal neuralgia
Management is medical with anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine first; sectioning of the nervus intermedius or microvascular decompression is reserved for refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Geniculate neuralgia is a paroxysmal neuralgia arising from the nervus intermedius, the sensory and parasympathetic division of the facial nerve, whose geniculate ganglion carries sensation from part of the external ear. Ectopic neural discharges, often attributed to vascular compression at the nerve root or to prior herpetic (varicella-zoster) inflammation of the geniculate ganglion, are thought to generate the intense deep-ear pain. Because the nervus intermedius also mediates taste, lacrimation, and salivation, attacks may be accompanied by disturbances of these functions, and its close relationship to the glossopharyngeal and trigeminal systems produces overlapping symptomatology.
additionalDifferentials: Primary otological disease (otitis externa or media)
Cerebellopontine angle or skull base tumour
additionalInvestigations: Otoscopy and microscopy to exclude middle and external ear disease
MRI of the internal auditory meatus and cerebellopontine angle with attention to the facial nerve
MR angiography to identify a compressive vascular loop
Assessment of the external auditory canal for a triggerable zone
Audiometry if hearing symptoms or tinnitus accompany the pain
Examination of the oropharynx to exclude referred otalgia from malignancy
redFlags: Vesicles in the ear canal or pinna with facial weakness suggesting Ramsay Hunt syndrome
Persistent unilateral otalgia with a normal ear, prompting a search for a head and neck primary
Progressive facial weakness or other cranial neuropathies
A cerebellopontine angle mass on imaging
reference.prognosis: Geniculate neuralgia is benign but can be highly distressing; many patients respond to anticonvulsant therapy, and surgical sectioning of the nervus intermedius or microvascular decompression offers relief in selected refractory cases.
pitfalls: Attributing deep ear pain to primary ear disease when the ear is normal
Failing to consider a herpetic (post-Ramsay Hunt) origin
Confusing it with glossopharyngeal neuralgia given the shared deep-ear pain
Not excluding referred otalgia from an oropharyngeal malignancy
Overlooking a treatable vascular loop or tumour on imaging
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: First-line medical therapy with anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine, with gabapentin or other neuropathic agents as alternatives
Consideration of antiviral therapy where a herpetic (varicella-zoster) aetiology or preceding Ramsay Hunt syndrome is implicated
Exclude other causes of deep ear pain with otoscopy, imaging of the internal auditory meatus and cerebellopontine angle, and examination for referred otalgia
Trigger-zone avoidance advice for provoking stimuli in the external auditory canal
Microvascular decompression of a compressive vascular loop or sectioning of the nervus intermedius and geniculate ganglion in refractory cases
Refer to neurology and skull-base neurosurgery or otolaryngology for drug-resistant or diagnostically uncertain disease
